analysis.one_liner: Bans hidden and excessive junk fees on hotel rooms, tickets, phone and internet bills, and airline extras.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 2025 with 3 cosponsors, the bill was referred to two House committees and has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require hotels, booking sites, ticket sellers, phone and internet companies, and airlines to show the full price of what you're buying up front, including mandatory fees. It would ban excessive or deceptive fees, stop phone and internet companies from charging early-termination fees, require prorated refunds when you cancel service, force ticket sellers to disclose how many tickets exist before sales open, and require airlines to report what they collect in bag, seat-selection, and change fees. The FTC and FCC would enforce the rules, and state attorneys general could sue violators.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers buying hotel rooms and vacation rentals, concert and sports tickets, phone and internet service, and plane travel, who today discover mandatory fees only at checkout and often cannot avoid them. Families get one clear total price before they commit, prorated credits when they cancel a phone or internet plan, full refunds when a ticket reseller can't deliver, and public data on how much airlines make from bag and seat fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers booking hotels, tickets, flights, and phone service

how_it_helps.text: Requires businesses to display the total price, including every mandatory fee and government charge, in ads and when a price is first shown, and bars the price from changing during checkout [S2].
Bans excessive or deceptive mandatory fees, with the FTC judging whether a fee is proportional to the actual cost of the service [S2].
Prohibits phone, internet, and cable providers from charging early-termination fees and requires prorated credits or rebates for unused days in a billing cycle after cancellation [S2].
Requires telecom bills and ads to show one clear aggregate price, and to disclose when an introductory price ends and what the regular rate will be [S2].

Requires ticket sellers to disclose the total number of tickets available at least 72 hours before public sale, disclose refund policies up front, refund the full fee-inclusive price on refunds, and warn buyers clearly when a reseller does not yet possess the ticket [S2].

Requires airlines to report quarterly to the Transportation Department, and the Department to publish, exactly how much revenue they collect from bag, change, cancellation, and seat-selection fees [S2].
Gives the FTC power to write rules on other hidden fees and allows state attorneys general to sue violators for injunctions, restitution, and damages on behalf of residents [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Hotels, vacation-rental platforms, ticket sellers and resale sites, broadband and wireless companies, and airlines, which would have to give up fee revenue that is currently disclosed only at checkout and absorb compliance costs for all-in pricing, billing changes, and quarterly airline reporting. Companies that rely on mandatory fees a reasonable customer would assume are already included in the sticker price would lose that revenue directly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hotels, ticket sellers, airlines, and telecom providers

drawbacks.text: The 'excessive fee' ban relies on judgment calls: the FTC and courts must weigh whether a fee is proportional to the cost of the service, which creates uncertainty for businesses about which fees are lawful and could invite litigation [S2].

All-in advertised pricing can make headline prices look higher even when the total is unchanged, and some businesses argue advertised all-in prices are harder to compare across markets with different local taxes and fees [S2].
Airline ancillary fees are addressed only through transparency reporting, not limits, so the bill discloses bag and seat-fee revenue without capping it [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to consumers are concrete and easy to understand: one honest total price before you buy, no penalty for canceling a phone plan, and full refunds when a resale ticket falls through. The main costs fall on businesses that currently earn revenue from mandatory fees added at checkout and on compliance burdens, especially the open-ended 'excessive fee' standard, which will require regulators to draw lines case by case. On balance the bill is a straightforward consumer-protection measure whose costs are real but narrow, aimed at pricing practices rather than the underlying services.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in December 2025 and sent to two House committees, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Janelle Bynum introduced the Junk Fee Prevention Act in the House on December 4, 2025 [S1].
The bill was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, as is routine when a bill spans jurisdictions [S4].
No committee action, hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history after the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained from the bill itself because it has not moved. Businesses that rely on mandatory fees added at checkout, including hotels, ticket sellers, airlines, and broadband providers, continue their current pricing practices while the bill sits without a hearing or vote.

industries.industry: Hotels, motels, and short-term rental platforms
industries.note: The bill requires lodging providers and booking sites to show one all-in price with every mandatory fee, eliminating resort and cleaning fees that appear only at checkout. Their gain from surprise fees comes directly out of travelers' budgets.

The bill bans excessive fees, requires full-fee refunds, and forces disclosure of how many tickets exist before a presale, ending opaque holdbacks that let scalpers resell seats fans never had a chance to buy. Speculative resellers that advertise tickets they don't hold must warn buyers and refund in full if they can't deliver.

Providers must end early-termination fees, prorate final bills, show one clear aggregate price on bills and in ads, and disclose when introductory rates expire and what the regular rate will be. Fees tacked onto advertised prices would be subject to FCC rules.

Airlines face only new reporting burdens: quarterly disclosure of ancillary fee revenue from bags, seat selection, changes, and cancellations. The bill does not cap these fees, so airlines keep charging them while consumers get public data on how much the fees raise.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with two committees and only three Democratic cosponsors nearly a month after introduction. With no bipartisan support and no committee movement, its most likely path is to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress unless it is attached to a larger consumer-protection package or the FTC's separate junk-fee rulemaking advances on its own.
